primary_category.subcategory: A2.4 Information search, retrieval, gathering, and evaluation

evidence.quote: I looked for anything from the cab — smoke, sparks, smell — didn't see or smell a thing. Told the dispatcher we copied the alarm...
evidence.explanation: The engineer actively seeks corroborating sensory evidence and evaluates the credibility of an automated alarm against detector history.

evidence.quote: I could have. The information's usually gettable if you push for it. I just didn't think it would've changed anything in the moment...
evidence.explanation: The worker weighs whether to retrieve additional diagnostic information (axle/car detail) from another party, a core information-evaluation act.

evidence.quote: Honestly, I leaned on what I've seen over the years... two alarms from detectors with that reputation — to me that still read as consistent with the pattern I already knew.
evidence.explanation: The engineer evaluates and compares new alarm evidence against a historical evidence base to decide its reliability.

evidence.quote: I did have him do a rolling check from his side window at the next spot where visibility was decent, just to cover myself on that first alarm.
evidence.explanation: The engineer devises a specific, situation-tailored intermediate verification step, combining timing, conductor deployment, and risk trade-off rather than following a single fixed rule.

evidence.quote: Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher, requested an unscheduled stop immediately.
evidence.explanation: Rapid non-routine resolution combining coordination and timing decisions in response to a novel, escalating situation.

evidence.quote: In eleven years running this territory, almost every hot-box call from these wet-weather detectors has turned out to be nothing.
evidence.explanation: The worker generalises from accumulated experience to build a mental model of detector reliability under specific weather conditions, applying it to interpret new events.

secondary_categories.subcategory: A2.1 Uncodified visual or auditory information processing

evidence.quote: conductor calls up and says he's smelling something acrid from the trailing end of the train.
evidence.explanation: Detection and interpretation of a non-codified perceptual cue (smell) that cannot be reduced to an explicit instrument reading, used to trigger an operational response.

evidence.quote: The conductor mentioned the ride felt a little rough through one stretch, but he chalked it up to rail joints.
evidence.explanation: Perceptual interpretation of an ambiguous physical sensation (ride quality) requiring judgment about its cause.

evidence.quote: Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher, requested an unscheduled stop immediately.
evidence.explanation: The engineer coordinates an operational response across roles (dispatcher, conductor, car department) to execute a safety-critical stop, organizing dependencies between parties.

evidence.quote: I did have him do a rolling check from his side window...
evidence.explanation: The engineer directs the conductor's action, coordinating a shared task toward a verification goal.

not_observed_or_insufficient: A1.1 Strength — no evidence of physical exertion or load handling.
A1.2 Dexterity — throttle/brake handling is referenced generically but no fine manual manipulation detail is described.
A1.3 Navigation — no description of the engineer physically moving through or orienting within an environment beyond operating the train from the cab.
A2.3 Numeracy — no explicit calculation, quantification, or numerical estimation is described beyond mileage/time references used narratively.
A3.1 Serving and attending — no customer or client-facing service interaction is depicted.
A3.2 Teaching, training, and coaching — the closing remark to a 'fresh crew' is advisory reflection, not an active teaching act within the episode.
A3.3 Selling and influencing — no persuasion or negotiation act is depicted.
A3.5 Caring — no welfare-oriented or health-support interaction is depicted.
ambiguities: The rolling visual check (decision point 2) could be classified as A1.2 Dexterity if physical operation of controls were emphasized, but the interview frames it purely as an information-gathering and planning act performed by the conductor, not a manual skill performed by the participant, so A1.2 was not assigned.

The closing advisory statement to a hypothetical 'fresh crew' borders on A3.2 Teaching but occurs outside the operational decision episode as a reflective closing remark, so it was excluded from secondary categories.

evidence.quote: My normal practice on this run, when nothing's confirmed wrong, is to just keep the plan as built — that's what I did.
evidence.explanation: The engineer independently decides speed, stopping, and verification actions without requiring approval, indicating high discretion over method and timing.

evidence.quote: dispatcher radios that the corridor's on-time numbers have been under review this month
evidence.explanation: Performance metrics (on-time numbers) are tracked and communicated by a supervising function (dispatch/corridor management), indicating an external monitoring influence, though not moment-to-moment supervision of the engineer's specific choices.

evidence.quote: working the radio with the dispatcher... I did have him do a rolling check from his side window... conductor calls up and says he's smelling something acrid...
evidence.explanation: The engineer regularly exchanges information and coordinates actions with the conductor and dispatcher, but each party performs distinct individual tasks rather than jointly executing a single shared physical task.

evidence.quote: I've had this territory for about eleven years now... I know of at least two times in the last six months it flagged something in wet weather that turned out to be nothing.
evidence.explanation: Recurring alarms and recurring meets/timing decisions on the same territory indicate a repeated task structure, though each incident required distinct judgment.

evidence.quote: Told the dispatcher we copied the alarm... Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher, requested an unscheduled stop immediately.
evidence.explanation: Alarm acknowledgment and emergency-stop protocols suggest prescribed communication procedures, though the interview does not fully specify a formal checklist being followed.

evidence.quote: hot bearing alarm, didn't specify which axle exactly, just flagged the train... this one specified roughly the same car position as before
evidence.explanation: The alarms provide ambiguous, incomplete information about a physical condition, and the true state of the equipment remains uncertain across multiple decision points.

evidence.quote: conductor calls up and says he's smelling something acrid from the trailing end of the train... Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher, requested an unscheduled stop immediately.
evidence.explanation: The engineer must respond immediately to an unplanned, escalating physical anomaly outside the standard operating plan.

tools.role_in_task: Wayside hot-bearing detector system generating automated alarms interpreted by the engineer.

evidence.quote: we passed a wayside detector and got the automated call — hot bearing alarm... second detector, independent from the first, flags a hot bearing alarm again
evidence.explanation: Wayside detectors are purpose-built railway sensor/monitoring systems, more specialised than ordinary office or communication ICT, and are central to the decision episode.

tools.role_in_task: Locomotive power, braking, and speed controls operated directly by the engineer.

evidence.quote: I'm the engineer, so I'm running the power, handling speed and braking...
evidence.explanation: The engineer directly operates digitally/electronically controlled locomotive equipment, consistent with non-autonomous digitally enabled machinery.

tools.role_in_task: Two-way radio communication with dispatcher and conductor.

evidence.quote: working the radio with the dispatcher... Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher
evidence.explanation: Radio is a digitally enabled communication tool central to coordinating the decision episode, but does not fit basic ICT (office software) or specialised ICT (professional analysis system) categories precisely.

task_anchors.task_description: Interpreting an ambiguous automated hot-bearing alarm using detector history and cab observation.
Maintaining the standing operating plan while directing a conductor rolling visual check as an interim verification measure.
Evaluating a second independent alarm against prior belief and schedule pressure, deciding to continue rather than inspect.
Responding to a direct physical hazard cue (smell) with an emergency stop coordinated via radio.

evidence: I looked for anything from the cab — smoke, sparks, smell — didn't see or smell a thing.
I did have him do a rolling check from his side window at the next spot where visibility was decent.
two alarms from detectors with that reputation — to me that still read as consistent with the pattern I already knew
Made an emergency radio call to the dispatcher, requested an unscheduled stop immediately.

missing_evidence: No direct description of manual control operation detail (e.g., throttle handle movements) to support a dexterity claim.
No numerical calculation shown explicitly, despite time/mileage references, so numeracy was not assigned.
